issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, in an appeal against acquittal under Article 136, has the power to interfere with findings of fact.

facts: The trial court had convicted the accused.
The High Court, on appeal, set aside the conviction and acquitted the accused, reasoning that the witnesses were not independent or impartial.
law: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court has the power to interfere with findings of fact in an appeal against acquittal.
The Court makes no distinction between its power in appeals against acquittal and appeals against conviction.
However, in cases of acquittal, the Court will not ordinarily interfere with the appreciation of evidence or findings of fact unless the High Court has acted "perversely or otherwise improperly."
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had no justification for dismissing what the Supreme Court considered to be "cogent evidence of a conclusive nature."
The Supreme Court determined that the High Court's reasoning for the acquittal—that the witnesses were not independent—was based on "mere conjectures" and was "without justification."
This improper dismissal of evidence by the High Court met the threshold for the Supreme Court to exercise its power of interference.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that it has the power under Article 136 to interfere with findings of fact in an appeal against acquittal, but it will only do so if the High Court has acted perversely or improperly. In this case, the Court found the High Court's reasoning for acquittal to be based on unjustified conjectures, and therefore it interfered, set aside the acquittal, and convicted the accused.

issue.issue_text: Whether the evidence relating to recoveries is legally similar to that contemplated under Section 103 of the Cr.P.C., requiring the same procedural safeguards as a matter of law.

facts: The lower court (High Court) had rejected evidence of recoveries because the witnesses were connected to the deceased and were not independent or impartial.

The lower court believed that the Investigating Officer should have called independent witnesses from the locality, similar to the procedure for a search, and found the use of the same witnesses for multiple recoveries to be objectionable.
law: The Court distinguished between a 'recovery' of evidence based on information from an accused and a 'search' as contemplated under Section 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.).
Section 103 Cr.P.C. requires that searches be conducted in the presence of two or more inhabitants of the locality where the search takes place.
application: The Supreme Court held that the strict procedural requirements of Section 103 Cr.P.C. do not apply to recoveries.
The Court stated that a recovery can be proven even by the solitary evidence of the Investigating Officer if their testimony is otherwise believable.
It explicitly rejected the notion that it could be laid down as a matter of law or practice that different sets of witnesses must be called for recoveries from different places.
In this specific case, the Court found it was proper for witnesses who worked with the deceased to be present, as they could identify the missing items.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that evidence relating to recoveries is not legally similar to a search under Section 103 Cr.P.C. and, therefore, does not require the same procedural safeguards as a matter of law, such as the mandatory presence of two or more independent local witnesses.

issue.issue_text: Whether the court, while considering evidence of recovery under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, must exercise caution and care to ensure the credibility of the information furnished by the accused.

law.fact_text: Section 27 of the Evidence Act makes information given by an accused in custody, which leads to the discovery of a fact, admissible as evidence.
law.law_text: Section 27 of the Evidence Act is liable to be abused by investigating officers through manipulation or ingenuity to circumvent the protections afforded to an accused under Sections 25 and 26 of the Act.

application.fact_text: The Court acknowledged the potential for abuse of Section 27 of the Evidence Act.
application.law_text: For this reason, the Court determined that great caution must be exercised when considering evidence of recovery under this section.

application.fact_text: The Court must evaluate the information furnished by the accused and the resulting discovery.
application.law_text: In doing so, the Court must exercise the necessary caution and care to lend assurance that the information furnished by the accused leading to the discovery is credible.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the proposition, holding that due to the potential for abuse and manipulation of Section 27 of the Evidence Act by investigating officers, a court must exercise great caution and care when considering recovery evidence. This scrutiny is necessary to ensure and lend assurance that the information provided by the accused is credible.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, in an appeal against acquittal under Article 136, has the power to interfere with findings of fact.
appellant_arguments: The High Court was not justified in acquitting the accused by 'jettisoning... cogent evidence of a conclusive nature on mere conjectures'.
respondent_arguments: The defense's role is to create 'uncertainty and doubt' regarding the prosecution's evidence, which is sufficient to give the benefit of the doubt to the accused, and the High Court's acquittal based on this should stand.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the evidence relating to recoveries is legally similar to that contemplated under Section 103 of the Cr.P.C., requiring the same procedural safeguards as a matter of law.
appellant_arguments: The evidence of recovery is admissible and valid without adhering to the procedural safeguards of Section 103 Cr.P.C. (inferred, as the appellant relied on the recoveries).
respondent_arguments: The evidence relating to recoveries should be subject to the same procedural safeguards as searches under Section 103 of the Cr.P.C. to be considered legally valid (inferred from the court's direct rejection of this legal proposition).

arguments.issue_text: Whether the court, while considering evidence of recovery under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, must exercise caution and care to ensure the credibility of the information furnished by the accused.
appellant_arguments: The recovery evidence is credible and unassailable, as items were recovered from the accused's room and person, and the accused's claim of signing blank papers is contradicted by the remand application.
respondent_arguments: The recovery evidence is not credible because the recovery memos were 'fake', the accused was made to sign 'three blank papers', and the investigating officer 'created evidence' and 'planted' items on the accused.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In an appeal against acquittal by special leave, the Supreme Court has the power to interfere with findings of fact, and will not ordinarily interfere with the appreciation of evidence or findings of fact unless the High Court acted perversely or otherwise improperly.
obiter: The information by an accused leading to the discovery of a witness to whom he had given stolen articles is a discovery of a fact within the meaning of Sec. 27.
The word 'fact' is not restricted to something which can be exhibited as a material object.
It is not the function of this Court to determine who other than the person who has been charged with the murder had committed it.
The penumbra of uncertainty in the evidence before a Court is generally due to the nature and quality of that evidence.

In our view the evidence in this case is sufficient to justify the conviction of the accused for an offence of murder.
